mcqs.question: Why does double buffering keep a GPU rendering pipeline running smoothly compared to single buffering?
options: It doubles the physical memory available on the graphics card
It eliminates the need to ever draw a new frame
Double buffering only works if the display refresh rate matches the frame rate exactly
The GPU can draw the next frame into one buffer while the display shows the completed previous frame, so production and consumption never wait on each other
mcqs.explanation: Double buffering overlaps drawing and displaying by using two buffers in alternating roles, so neither the GPU nor the display has to wait for the other mid-frame. It doesn't add physical memory capacity system-wide, doesn't eliminate drawing, and works across a range of refresh-rate/frame-rate relationships, not just an exact match.

mcqs.question: Why are circular (ring) buffers the standard structure for network interface card receive queues, rather than a simple double buffer?
options: Ring buffers physically consume less memory than any other structure
NICs cannot use any buffer with more than 2 slots
A ring buffer generalizes to N slots with independent read/write pointers, handling bursty or variable-rate arrival without needing a fixed two-buffer swap
Double buffers are only usable for video, never for network data
mcqs.explanation: A ring buffer's N-slot design with chasing pointers adapts naturally to bursts and variable rates, which is exactly what network packet arrival looks like — unlike a fixed two-buffer swap tuned for a steady, alternating pattern. Memory footprint depends on slot count and size, not an inherent ring-buffer advantage, and there's no such NIC restriction.

mcqs.question: Why does free -h on a healthy Linux system often show very little RAM as literally "free"?
options: This indicates a memory leak that needs to be fixed
The kernel deliberately uses otherwise-idle RAM for the page cache, which is instantly reclaimable if an application needs it
Linux reserves most RAM permanently for the kernel itself and it can never be used by applications
The measurement is a well-known bug in the free command
mcqs.explanation: Using idle RAM for the page cache is a deliberate performance optimization, not a leak or a bug — the kernel reclaims cached pages instantly when an application actually needs the memory. Low 'free' with high 'cache' is normal and healthy, not a sign of reserved or wasted memory.

mcqs.question: Why do most general-purpose operating systems default to write-back caching rather than write-through?
options: Write-back is the only policy that works with SSDs
Write-through cannot be implemented in software
Write-back gives fast write() latency for the common case where instant durability isn't needed, while write-through pays disk latency on every single write
Write-back guarantees stronger durability than write-through
mcqs.explanation: Write-back optimizes for the common case — most writes don't need to be instantly durable — by deferring the actual disk write. Write-through is implementable in software and works on any storage type; it's simply slower because every write pays disk latency immediately. Write-back is actually the weaker durability guarantee, not the stronger one.

mcqs.question: An application calls write() successfully, then the machine loses power one second later before any explicit sync. What can you say about that data?
options: It is guaranteed to be safe on disk, since write() reported success
It is guaranteed to be lost, since write() never touches disk directly
It depends only on the file's size, not on caching or flush timing
It may or may not have reached disk — write() only guarantees the data reached the page cache, not that it was flushed to stable storage
mcqs.explanation: write() success means the data is in the page cache and visible to other reads on the machine, but the actual disk flush is asynchronous and could happen before or after the crash. Without an fsync(), there's a genuine window where success was reported but the data never became durable — it's not guaranteed either way.

mcqs.question: Why would a database engine like PostgreSQL choose to open its data files with O_DIRECT, bypassing the OS page cache?
options: O_DIRECT is required by the POSIX standard for all database software
The database implements its own caching logic tuned to its access patterns, and wants to avoid the OS redundantly caching the same data a second time, wasting RAM
O_DIRECT makes every I/O operation faster with no trade-offs
It's the only way to read a file larger than available RAM
mcqs.explanation: O_DIRECT lets an application that already manages its own smart caching avoid double-buffering the same data through the generic OS page cache. It's a genuine trade-off, not a free speedup — it adds alignment requirements and loses OS-provided read-ahead — and it's not required by any standard, nor needed just to read large files.
